name: Transitional serif
summary: The Enlightenment roman between the old style and the Didone: the stress turns nearly vertical, the contrast rises, and the serifs become flatter and sharper. It is precise but still warm, and it reads well in text.

philosophy.core_thesis: A letter can be drawn by reason and still serve the reader: the pen gives way to the engraver's line, but not yet to the extreme.
design_principles: Keep the stroke contrast between 2.5:1 and 4.5:1, measured on the lower-case o.
Set the stress vertical or within 10° of it.
Give the serifs a short bracket and flat, level head serifs on the lower case.
Make the round letters wide and the bowls full: the o is close to a circle in the lower case.
Hold the x-height at 0.60–0.70 of the cap height.
Use ball terminals on a, c, f, g and r, smaller than in a Didone.
anti_patterns: A strong diagonal stress from a broad-nib pen
Hairlines finer than 0.15 of the stem in text sizes
Unbracketed, hairline serifs at a right angle to the stem
Tracking tighter than −0.01 em in text

classification.note: The line to the Garalde is the stress angle; the line to the Didone is the bracket. A face with hairline serifs and no bracket is a Didone.

anatomy.contrast: Clear: the thin parts are 0.22–0.4 of the stem.
anatomy.stress: Vertical or nearly vertical, within 10°; the thinnest parts of the o are at 12 and 6 o'clock.
anatomy.serifs: Bracketed, flat and sharp; the head serifs of the lower case are almost level.
anatomy.terminals: Ball or teardrop terminals on a, c, f and r; the ear of the g is horizontal.
anatomy.aperture: Moderate: the c and e are less open than in a Garalde.
anatomy.key_letters: A g with an open lower loop (in Baskerville), a W without a middle serif, and a Q with a long, curved tail.

metrics.x_height: The x-height is 0.60–0.70 of the cap height and about 0.43–0.53 of the em.
metrics.contrast: The side of the o is 2.5 to 4.5 times as thick as its top.
metrics.width: Round letters are wide; the mean advance of a to z is 0.48–0.58 em.
metrics.figures: Old-style figures in text in the original; many revivals give lining figures by default.

setting.text_sizes: Set text at 10–12 pt in print and 16–20 px on screen.
setting.display_sizes: Use it up to 48 pt; above that the hairlines can look weak against the stems.
setting.leading: Set the leading at 1.3–1.5 times the size for text, and 1.1–1.2 for titles.
setting.tracking: Set 0 em tracking in text; letter-space capitals by 0.04–0.08 em.
setting.case_and_features: Use the italic for emphasis; the transitional italic has an even slope of 12–16°.

pairing.rule: Pair it with a sans of a rational, upright skeleton, or with its own italic; keep the x-heights within 5%.

pairs.role: sans for interface, captions and data
pairs.why: Both have a vertical stress and a rational build, so they share an order without a fight.
The Didone is the next step of the same idea, so the titles feel like a sharper version of the text.

reference_faces.note: Libre Baskerville has a larger x-height (about 0.69) for screens; Baskervville stays closer to the original (about 0.61).

evidence.title: A specimen by John Baskerville of Birmingham
evidence.credit: Cambridge University Library, Fleuron record; scan on Wikimedia Commons

emotion.target_response: Confidence and clarity: the reader feels an educated voice that is exact but not cold.

avoid_when: The brief asks for a loose, handmade or playful voice.
The text sits under 11 px on a screen.

modifiers.how: Remove the brackets, take the hairlines down to 0.1 of the stem, and use it only at display sizes.
Tilt the stress 15–20°, lower the contrast to 2.5:1, and use old-style figures.

sources.title: Robert Bringhurst, The Elements of Typographic Style (Hartley & Marks, 4th ed. 2012)
